extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical poetics, literary critics, poets, and scholars of Aristotle/Poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative principles and defenses for poetry drawn from Aristotle (as explained/commented here): what counts as fault or excellence in imitation, diction, character, and poetic method. Intended to guide critics and poets in judging poetic choices (truth, verisimilitude, genre-appropriateness, diction, context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault: factual ignorance vs vicious imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's error from ignorance (e.g. describing a doe with horns) is more pardonable than a vicious imitation; the former proceeds from ignorance of a truth of nature while the latter is a failure in the poet's art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the poet simply errs about a natural fact, critics may excuse him (Aristotle's example: a doe with horns). But deliberate or bad imitation that departs from the poet's own art is a graver fault. Distinguish ignorance-based slip from a deficiency in imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three legitimate modes of poetic representation (as are / as ought to be / as is reported)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may treat a subject as it is, as it ought to be, or as it is said to be; representation falling under none of these authorities is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use verisimilitude (probability), necessity, or report/fame to justify departures from literal truth. If a poet represents things 'as they ought to be' (idealised) that can defend otherwise improbable descriptions; if representing 'as is' he should follow necessity and closeness to copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriateness: imitate what nature could do vs what she did
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres call for different standards: tragedy and epic should imitate what is most excellent (what nature could do), comedy should more closely imitate what actually happens (what nature did).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sophocles aimed to make heroes 'as they ought to be' (idealized) while Euripides made them 'as they were' (more realistic); choose the mode fitting the genre's aims and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recourse to fame/report as justification
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject is neither probable nor necessary, appeal to report (fame/tradition) to justify the poet's account (e.g., Homer following earlier poets' reports about the gods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior authoritative report or common tradition can excuse a poet's account even if it's not literally true; check whether earlier poets or common belief supported the depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegorical reading (theological, natural, moral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic depictions of gods or wonders can be allegorical (theological, natural, or moral), and thus not literal assertions about divinity or nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret divine actions as representing theological truths, natural causes, or moral allegories; this can defend apparent improprieties in depiction (e.g., gods with human passions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect to customs and historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem should be judged against the customs and practices of the poet's time; what seems wrong by later/customary standards may be regular in the poet's era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics must avoid imposing their own age's customs on ancient poets; check historical customs (e.g., how soldiers kept pikes) before condemning a passage as impossible or absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the speaker and the addressee (character-appropriate speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an utterance is good depends on who speaks and to whom: what is plausible or admirable for one character may be foolish coming from another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dialogue and tales in light of the speaker's character and the intended audience within the poem (e.g., songs suited to effeminate or rustic audiences). Don't conflate narrator/character voice with authorial endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of circumstances (persons, time, place, means, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge a passage with full regard to its circumstances — the persons involved, time, place, means used, and the end/purpose — since these can transform something apparently bad into something good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before condemning actions or descriptions, examine situational particulars (purpose, cultural norms, intended effect); many otherwise offensive passages are justified by circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal appropriateness / conjuncture of time
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular time or conjuncture in the narrative can render conduct, speech, or episodic length acceptable; timing affects propriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An episode's placement (e.g., after the removal of a powerful adversary) may justify long digressions or conversational scenes that would be inappropriate elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means and diction justify extraordinary character behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The methods or means poets use to unfold the fable (including diction, metaphor, and narrative devices) can justify characters' seemingly extraordinary or cruel behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraordinary acts or humiliations in character may be necessary for the subject and be justified by how the poet handles the means of exposition; consider narrative necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ends (poetic purpose) can justify means
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem's intended end (its moral, pedagogical, or aesthetic purpose) may justify means that seem low or humiliating in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the outcome or overall moral/poetic aim demands certain scenes or degradations, those means can be excused; evaluate in light of the work's end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction comprises thought and expression; richness can excuse critics
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction includes both thoughts and expression; a poet's mastery of language (richness, apt metaphors) can rebut critics' objections about particular words or passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer's excellence in expression and thought can excuse peculiarities. Evaluate the richness and functions of diction (e.g., metaphorical uses, elevated phrasing) before faulting a passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for dialectal/foreign meanings and accents
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent linguistic blunders may be explained by dialectal or foreign meanings, alternate senses, or accentuation differences, so a word thought improper might have a justifying sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before condemning on lexical grounds, check variant, foreign, or dialect senses (e.g., a word meaning 'guard' vs 'mule'); accent and regional usage may salvage a line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor and figurative speech are permissible and often necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphorical or figurative language (e.g., 'he cast his eyes' meaning 'he thought') is common and defensible in poetry; attributing voice to mute things or using metaphorical verbs is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and accept metaphors, synecdoche, and other figurative tropes as standard poetic devices; relate them to scriptural and other high-authority uses to justify their force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish narrator/poet from character viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's text may contain statements attributable to characters, singers, or narrators rather than to the poet himself; criticisms must note whose voice is at stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a scandalous or improbable claim is the utterance of a character (e.g., a minstrel at a feast) — such a viewpoint can explain or justify the content as illustrative rather than endorsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and length of episodes must be judged by narrative function
rubrics_metrics.description: Long episodes or digressions (which critics call excessive) can serve functions: provide relief, diversify the poem, praise characters, or introduce allegory — and so may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate episodic length/placement by what it accomplishes in the narrative (resting the reader, praising a hero, inserting allegory). Don't judge length in isolation from narrative purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precedent/authority to excuse content
rubrics_metrics.description: If earlier poets or authorities used a form or tale, later poets can be justified in following that precedent (e.g., Homer following Orpheus and predecessors regarding the gods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether a motif or depiction is traditional; continuity with respected predecessors weakens charges of ignorance or impropriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anachronistic judgment — prefer historical/philological inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics who demand conformity to later manners or to a different era's norms are unjust; rigorous critics should study the language, customs, and interpretive traditions of the poet's time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use philological, antiquarian, and contextual inquiry (customs, poetic meter, oral practice) before making condemnations; judges must be modest and reserved.
